progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: chem-m7-c10 (esterification: the acid loses OH, the alcohol loses H, water leaves; the ester group –COO–; condensation reaction; the cut line); chem-m7-c11 (amines, the –NH₂ group; the amide link, C=O bonded to N; amide formation by condensation); chem-m7-c14 (monomer, polymer, repeat unit, brackets, n, continuation bonds; the chain view; dispersion contact; thermoplastic; HDPE about 130 °C; "Addition: nothing lost"); chem-m7-c05 and c03 (hydrogen bonding needs an H on N or O and a lone pair on N or O); chem-m7-c08b (polar C=O, dipole–dipole); chem-m7-c01 (naming; locants such as 1,2- and 1,6-). Not assumed: diol, dicarboxylic acid, diamine, condensation polymerisation, polyester, polyamide, nylon 6,6, PET, hydrolysis.
progression.startsWith: Join monomers through ester or amide links. The video opens: Last time, every atom of every monomer ended up in the chain. A PET drink bottle is different. Every time two of its monomers join, a small molecule of water comes off.
progression.stopsAfter: explaining why condensation monomers need two reactive ends; forming PET and nylon 6,6; drawing a condensation repeat unit; recovering the monomers; comparing addition and condensation by monomer, by-product, repeat-unit formula and backbone link; explaining nylon's and PET's properties and uses from their structure. No acid chloride route, no natural polymers, no lifecycle.
progression.nextLesson: polymer practice from both families (route chem-m7-g04, "Polymer practice: repeating units, monomers and properties").

teaching.task: Make polyethylene, and every atom of every monomer ends up in the chain. Make a PET bottle or a nylon rope, and a water molecule comes off at every link. How do two-ended monomers build a condensation polymer, how do you draw its repeat unit and get the monomers back, and how do its ester and amide links give PET and nylon their properties?
teaching.causalExplanation: (1) addition kept every atom; PET and nylon lose water at each link (1); (2) one reactive group makes one small molecule and stops; a group at each end keeps a reactive end after every link, so the chain grows both ways (2); (3) PET: the acid loses OH, the alcohol loses H, water leaves, an ester link forms, again and again: condensation polymerisation, a polyester (3); (4) the repeat unit is one of each monomer minus the water at each end; the ends are complementary; two ester links per unit (4); (5) a diamine in place of the diol gives amide links: nylon 6,6, a polyamide (5); (6) adding the water back splits each link and gives the monomers; count the C=O carbons (6); (7) comparison: monomer, by-product, repeat-unit formula, backbone link; hydrolysis splits ester and amide links, usually slowly (7); (8) nylon's N–H and C=O hydrogen bond between chains: tough, high melting; amide links survive melting (8); (9) PET's stiff rings and polar ester links: strong, stiff, high melting; bottles and fibres (9); memory aid (10); two attempts and brief feedback (11 to 14); handoff (15); key notes (16).
teaching.conversationalApproach: the last video's addition polymers kept every atom, but a PET bottle loses a small molecule of water every time two monomers join, and nylon rope is made the same way, so the video asks how a chain can grow while losing something at every link and what those links do to the plastic. Esterification joins an acid and an alcohol and stops, because ethyl ethanoate has no spare group; a diol and a dicarboxylic acid each have a reactive group at both ends, so after one link the molecule can keep joining. PET forms from ethane-1,2-diol and benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid as water leaves at each ester link: condensation polymerisation, making a polyester. The repeat unit is one diol and one acid joined, water gone from each end, bracketed with continuation bonds and n. Swapping the diol for hexane-1,6-diamine gives amide links and nylon 6,6, a polyamide. Going backwards, adding the water back at each link recovers the monomers, counting both C=O carbons. Addition needs a C=C and loses nothing; condensation needs two reactive ends and loses water at every link. Nylon's N-H and C=O groups hydrogen bond between chains, so it melts near 265 degrees, while PET has no hydrogen bonds between chains but stiff rings and polar ester links. Two exam questions follow with brief feedback.
teaching.openingDecision: Last time, every atom of every monomer ended up in the chain. A PET drink bottle is different. Every time two of its monomers join, a small molecule of water comes off. Nylon rope is made the same way. So how can you build a long chain while losing something at every link, and what do those links do to the plastic?
teaching.understandingCheck: (A1) "Butane-1,4-diol, HO(CH₂)₄OH, reacts with butanedioic acid, HOOC(CH₂)₂COOH, to form a condensation polymer. (a) Draw the repeat unit of this polymer. (b) Name the type of link formed and the other product of the reaction." New monomers (the scene uses PET and the recovery example); tests scene 4's method and the by-product. Crossed mistake: "[–O–(CH₂)₄–O–CO–(CH₂)₂–CO–OH]ₙ" (an OH left at the bracket end; site Common Error "water retained"). (A2) "A polyamide has the repeat unit [–NH–(CH₂)₆–NH–CO–(CH₂)₈–CO–]ₙ. (a) Identify the two monomers used to make this polymer. (b) This polyamide melts at a much higher temperature than high-density polyethylene (HDPE). Explain this difference in terms of the forces between the polymer chains." New polymer (nylon 6,10); tests scene 6's recovery and scene 8's cause. Crossed mistake: "octanedioic acid" (the two C=O carbons not counted; site WE2's trap).
teaching.curriculumScope: Syllabus (NSW Chemistry Stage 6, 2017), as printed: "model and compare the structure, properties and uses of condensation polymers, for example:; nylon; polyesters" This video covers why a condensation monomer needs a reactive group at each end, how PET (a polyester) and nylon 6,6 (a polyamide) form with water released at every link, drawing a condensation repeat unit, recovering the monomers by adding the water back, comparing addition and condensation (monomer, by-product, backbone link, repeat-unit formula), and how hydrogen bonding (nylon) and stiff rings with polar ester links (PET) set their properties and uses. Addition polymers are chem-m7-c14; mixed practice is chem-m7-g04 (route review change 4). this video starts by joining monomers through ester or amide links, and stops at comparing repeat units and small-molecule by-products, with the property links that route review change 4 folds in. It teaches: esterification (c10) joins two molecules and releases water, but a monomer with one reactive group gives one small ester and stops; a monomer with a reactive group at each end (a diol, a dicarboxylic acid, a diamine) still has a reactive end after each link forms, so the chain grows from both ends; PET from ethane-1,2-diol and benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid (terephthalic acid): at each link the acid loses OH and the alcohol loses H, they leave as water, and an ester link forms; condensation polymerisation (a polymer formed with a small molecule, usually water, released at every link); polyester (a polymer with ester links along its chain); the repeat unit: one diol plus one diacid, minus the water at each end, in brackets with a continuation bond through each bracket and n outside; the end check (the right-hand C=O carbon bonds to an oxygen like the one on the left); two ester links per repeat unit; nylon 6,6 from hexane-1,6-diamine and hexanedioic acid, the amide link (c11), polyamide, "6,6" for the six carbons in each monomer; monomers from a repeat unit: cut each ester or amide link between the C=O carbon and the O or N, add OH to the C=O side and H to the O or N side; count the C=O carbons when naming the acid; comparison with addition: the monomer (C=C against a reactive group at each end), the by-product (none against water at every link), the repeat-unit formula (same as the monomer against the monomers minus two waters), and the backbone (all carbon against ester or amide links); hydrolysis named in one sentence (water can split ester and amide links, the reverse of condensation; usually slow without acid, base or an enzyme; a carbon backbone has no such weak point); nylon: the N–H of one chain hydrogen bonds to the C=O of a neighbouring chain, so the chains attract strongly: tough fibres, melting at about 265 °C (HDPE about 130 °C); still a thermoplastic: heating lets the chains slide, and the amide links in the chains do not break; PET: no N–H, so no hydrogen bonds between chains, but flat, stiff benzene rings stop the chains twisting and the polar ester links add dipole–dipole attraction: strong and stiff, melting at about 260 °C; bottles (tough, clear) and polyester fibres. Not here: the acid chloride route and HCl as a by-product (author note a; the narration says "a small molecule", and "here water" for the pairs shown); the 2n − 1 count of water molecules for a finite chain (a grey screen tag only); nylon 6 and other single-monomer condensation polymers (chem-m7-g04 uses PLA in Q3); proteins, polysaccharides and natural polymers (site L22 card 3 aside and L23 card 8, beyond the 2017 dotpoint; site correction 6 in `chem-m7-c14.md`); Kevlar, polycarbonate and PMMA (L23, extension); recycling codes, microplastics, PETase and bioplastics (route review change 4; author note d); reaction conditions and catalysts for PET and nylon (author note b); glass transition and crystallinity (author note c); thermosets (c14's grey chip covers them).

design.visualSystem: Explainer engine: warm paper stage, handwritten Caveat headings, amber doodle layer. Colour key as chem-m7-c10 and c11, with c14's polymer additions: carbon skeleton ink; hydrogens soft grey; oxygen brick red; nitrogen indigo with the letter N printed; the ester group ringed red; the amide group ringed red at the C=O and indigo at the N; reactive end groups ringed amber while they are being counted (end tags); released water in the Module 5 water colour; brackets, n and continuation bonds navy; benzene rings ink with a grey inner ring; chains in the chain view pale blue; dispersion contact dotted pale blue; hydrogen bonds dotted violet; dipole–dipole dotted teal; heat glow amber. Board layout (constant): top-left the short task chip ("Two ends", "Build PET", "Draw it", "Nylon", "Backwards", "Compare", "Why strong?"); centre the structure board or the chain view box, one model at a time; plates small or medium at the left or right only in scenes 1, 3, 5, 8, 9, 14 and 15. Clutter rule: at most three text items bright at once; every label fades when its sentence ends; the previous model leaves before the next one draws. Reuse: painted plates (inspected 28 Oct): `m7-polymer-objects-v1.png` (2000 × 2000; scenes 1 and 15, medium); `m7-hdpe-crate-v1.png` (2000 × 2000, a blue stackable crate; scene 8 and feedback 2, small). Not used: `m7-ester-fruit-v1.png` (a banana, pineapple and pear; c10's ester hook, not a polymer object); c14's other plates (addition polymers). Three new plates (Assets). All plates scaled uniformly only, never stretched or cropped. No human figures.
